# DECISIONS: iTaK Gaming

## 2026-10-15: A build is not family-ready until it runs on the real device
- **Decided:** No build is cleared for family use until the shipped app has been run on the real target device and at least one game launched without returning to the home screen (now TODO T-3.3).
- **Why:** Build 56 was cleared and shipped, then crashed on every launch on the real TV and its clearance was revoked; builds 57 to 61 fixed the crashes. Emulator and build-machine proof is not device proof.
- **Supersedes:** clearing builds on build-machine verification alone
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-15: Mail the stick on build 1.61; 1.62 comes from the update feed
- **Decided:** The family stick shipped to Mary and Terry in Missouri with build 1.61 (build 62) aboard after device testing showed correct picture; build 1.62 with the speed passes and the white menu bar is live on the update feed and offers itself when the stick goes online.
- **Why:** 1.61 was proven on the device; waiting longer delayed the gift for speed work the update feed delivers anyway.
- **Supersedes:** holding the stick until all speed work finished
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-12: No server-side game delivery, ever
- **Decided:** iTaK Gaming never serves or streams games to other people. Netplay relays inputs and signals only; both sides run the same core and ROM locally.
- **Why:** Lawsuit risk in delivering other people's games from our server.
- **Supersedes:** any server-side delivery design
- **By:** David

## 2026-10-11: Open source under MIT, no ROMs or core binaries in the repo
- **Decided:** The project is public under MIT at github.com/David2024patton/itak-gaming. The repo ships no ROMs and no core binaries; built apps obtain or bundle cores outside the source tree.
- **Why:** David's call to open the project while keeping game content and third-party binaries out of it.
- **Supersedes:** none
- **By:** David

# ENDGOAL: iTaK Gaming

The end state this project exists to reach, in plain words. TODO.md and PLAN.md are how we get here; this file is how we know we are done. Work continues until this end goal is reached. When David restates or extends the end goal, this file is updated the same day and PLAN/TODO follow.

## The end state

iTaK Gaming is the family arcade on every screen in the house and beyond it: a TV stick, a stronger TV box, a Windows or Linux machine, all running the same open-source arcade. Anyone in the family picks up a remote or controller, picks their profile, picks a system and a game, and plays, with their own save states waiting where they left them. David in Kentucky opens a lobby and plays his brother in Missouri like they are on the same couch, with family watching as spectators. Updates arrive on their own and verify themselves. The box in Mary and Terry's house in Missouri runs the same arcade, set up from the kit, recoverable from a one-page card by a family member with no developer help.

## How we will know it is reached

- The shipped app runs on the real Chromecast HD and every target device, and a game launches and plays without returning to the home screen, proven per build on the device itself.
- The Kentucky to Missouri acceptance game is played over the public lobby with a dated session note: build, game, connection path, desync count, result.
- Every bundled core carries a standard proof pack, and retail-game status is recorded separately from homebrew proof for the 64-bit cores.
- Spectators, friends, play stats, and leaderboards work in the live lobby service over TLS.
- A family member completes setup and a failed-update recovery from the written kit and card without developer help.
- The release gate passes clean on the release commit: tests, lint, secret scan, leak check, save compatibility, and netplay determinism.
- The repo stays clean in public: MIT code, and a tree leak check with every release finds no ROMs, BIOS files, core binaries, private logs, or credentials.

## Not in the end state

- No server-side game delivery or streaming of games to other people, ever. The server carries lobbies, signals, inputs, stats, friends, and updates only.
- No ROMs or core binaries shipped in the repo or the app packages; players supply their own legally obtained games.
- No pop-up ads in any build. Banner ads only in a build whose per-build core license manifest proves every bundled core allows that revenue model.

==================== FILE: MISSOURI-KIT.md ====================

# iTaK Gaming — Missouri Setup Kit

Everything needed to set up the arcade box at Mom's house in Missouri,
plus the short list of things to do to THIS box (the Death Star
Chromecast) before it travels.

## What's in the kit

- `iTaKGaming-<version>.apk` — the app installer (also updates itself
  afterwards, see Updates).
- This file.
- The ROM folders to copy onto the box (David supplies these from
  `C:\ROMs` on his PC; they are not in the public repo on purpose).

## Before the box leaves Kentucky (do at David's house)

1. **Disable Tailscale key expiry for the Chromecast** in the
   Tailscale admin console (Machines → Death Star → Disable key
   expiry). If the key expires in Missouri, remote support access
   dies with it.
2. Make sure the box is on the latest build: open iTaK Gaming,
   Settings → App updates. The footer on the Home screen shows the
   version (v1.0.40 or newer).
3. Confirm player profiles are set up (David at minimum) and the
   controller pairs and is assigned to a player (Players → pick a
   player → Assign controller → press a button on the pad).
4. Copy the ROM folders over (below) and open each system once to
   check the games show up.

## Setting up the box in Missouri

1. Plug the Chromecast into the TV (HDMI + USB power). Connect it to
   the house Wi-Fi.
2. If the app is not already on the box: put the kit APK on a USB
   stick or download it on the box, open it, and allow the install.
   The first time the app updates itself, Android asks once to allow
   installs from iTaK Gaming — tap Allow (one time per box).
3. ROMs live on the box at `/sdcard/ROMs/` in one folder per system:
   `NES`, `SNES`, `Genesis`, `GameBoy` (.gb/.gbc), `GBA` (.gba),
   `PS1` (.cue/.iso), `Dreamcast`. Drop the files in with any file
   manager (or `adb push`), then reopen the app; counts on the Home
   screen show what it found.
4. PlayStation and Sega CD games also want their BIOS files (the
   console's own firmware, supplied by the player) in
   `/sdcard/iTaK/system/`. Without one, PlayStation still runs most
   things on its built-in fallback BIOS.
5. Pair the Bluetooth controller in Android TV settings, then assign
   it to a player inside the app (see step 3 above).

## Playing online (Kentucky ↔ Missouri)

- Both boxes need internet. Open the Online tab: one side taps
  Create lobby, picks the game, optionally sets a password; the
  other side taps the lobby in the list. Both players must own the
  same game file.
- You land in a waiting room that shows both players. Each player
  taps READY; when both are ready there is a 5 second countdown and
  the game starts, in sync on both TVs.
- Pausing is safe: opening the menu tells the other side, the game
  waits, and their screen shows who paused. Closing the menu picks
  right back up.
- Cheats and save/load are off during online games (both sides must
  match exactly); your play time still counts on the leaderboard.

## Updates

The app updates itself. New builds are published to
`https://arcade.itak.live` and every box offers the update on its
Home screen ("Update now"), or check manually in Settings → App
updates. Nobody needs this kit again for updates.

## If something misbehaves

- Settings → Logs → Save a copy writes the debug log to
  `/sdcard/iTaK/`. Send that file to David; it records what the app
  did, including the emulator.
- Do NOT factory reset the box (it wipes the app, the ROMs, the
  saves and the wireless debugging pairing).
- The box's name on the network: Death Star, 192.168.0.247 on
  David's LAN (Missouri will give it a different address; Tailscale
  is the stable way in).

## The gift

This box is the family arcade: David in Kentucky, his brother and
Mom in Missouri, same game, same screen, over the internet. It
started as a surprise for Mary and Terry and grew into iTaK Gaming,
open source at https://github.com/David2024patton/itak-gaming
(the repo ships no games and no console firmware; those live on the
boxes, where they belong).

# PLAN: iTaK Gaming

The whole plan for iTaK Gaming, step by step. Sections are numbered S1, S2, ... and each build step names the TODO.md phase it maps to; every TODO item points back with (PLAN S<n>). When the plan changes, this file changes first, then TODO.md follows. Facts only: what is decided is stated, what is open is named as an open question.

## S1: What it is

iTaK Gaming is a family arcade for the living room. A Flutter TV frontend and a Go emulator host let each player pick a system, pick a game, and play with separate profiles and save states. Builds are made per platform instead of carrying every system in every package.

The project is open source under MIT. The repo ships no ROMs and no core binaries. Players supply their own legally obtained games and any required system firmware. Online play uses public lobbies and local execution on both sides; the server never serves or streams a game.

## S2: Architecture

| Module | What it owns |
| :--- | :--- |
| `flutter_ui` | TV-first screens: home, system select, game grid, players, online lobbies, leaderboard, settings, logs, update offers, avatars, and the TV keyboard |
| `go_backend` | Emulator host, libretro bridge, native Go core links, video, audio, input, save states, local API, and headless test tools |
| `cores/go-*` | Clean-room Go emulator cores, one module per system, with chip, video, audio, cartridge or disc, system, and test packages |
| `netplay` | Public lobby rendezvous, WebSocket signaling, lockstep relay rules, spectators, friends, play stats, leaderboards, and app distribution metadata |
| Platform builds | Android 32-bit for Chromecast HD, Android 64-bit for stronger TV boxes, Windows 64-bit, and Linux 64-bit; each build carries only the systems that fit it |
| Update feed | Version metadata and APK delivery with SHA-256 verification through the app update flow |

## S3: Hold the legal and repo foundation (TODO Phase 0)

MIT code, no ROMs or core binaries in Git, no server-side game delivery, and a per-build license manifest that says exactly which cores a build carries and whether that build may carry revenue.

## S4: Finish the TV shell (TODO Phase 1)

Separate feature modules for home, game grid, players, online, leaderboard, settings, logs, updates, avatars, and TV keyboard, then the weather home scene, screensaver, and token-free crash reporting. App models use built_value.dart (google/built_value.dart, BSD-3-Clause) for immutable value types and generated serialization of catalog and save data. Any in-app machine learning comes from flutter-mediapipe (google/flutter-mediapipe, Apache-2.0) pub packages instead of hand-rolled platform FFI.

## S5: Keep replacing and proving emulator cores (TODO Phase 2)

Clean-room Go modules, one per system, each with a standard proof pack and an honest retail-game status. Homebrew proof and retail proof are recorded separately; no core is called retail-proven on homebrew alone.

## S6: Ship per-platform builds only after real-device proof (TODO Phase 3)

Profile-driven speed work stays ahead of new features on the weak stick. Device QA runs on artemis (google/artemis, Apache-2.0), which drives real Android phones and TVs from natural-language test flows with Logcat and screenshots, and on cloud-android-orchestration (google/cloud-android-orchestration, Apache-2.0) as a Cuttlefish device farm for automated APK testing. bundletool (google/bundletool, Apache-2.0) builds the device-specific APK sets from one bundle and validates what will actually install.

## S7: Complete the lobby as the family online room (TODO Phase 4)

Two-player lockstep first, spectators and friends around it, then the real Kentucky to Missouri acceptance game. Game state never lives on the server; both sides run the same core and ROM locally and exchange inputs.

## S8: Make family deployment boring (TODO Phase 5)

Self-updates, the Missouri kit, recovery cards, and an in-person setup check in the house where the box will live.

## S9: Gate every release (TODO Phase 6)

Tests, lint, secret scanning, leak checks, save compatibility, netplay determinism, and the exact core license manifest. Banner ads stay out until the manifest proves the build allows them; pop-up ads never ship.

## S10: Standing boundaries

- No ROMs, BIOS files, or core binaries are committed to this repo.
- No server-side game delivery or game streaming to other people, ever.
- A build is not ready because it compiles. It is ready after the shipped app runs on the target device and a game launches.
- Own-core speed is measured on the actual Chromecast HD. The hardware is not blamed when a profile points at the core.
- Banner ads are allowed only for a build whose bundled core licenses allow that revenue model. Pop-up ads are not allowed.

## S11: Open questions

- Which home screen editing model should ship: auto-hide, full edit mode, or both? (owner: David)
- Should voice chat move from research into a build, starting with a USB microphone? (owner: David)
- What is the ship order for retail-game proof on the 64-bit cores? (owner: David and the build schedule)
- When will the Kentucky to Missouri acceptance game be played? (owner: David and his brother)

<div align="center">

# iTaK Gaming

A family arcade for the living room: pick a system, pick a game, play on the TV.

![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-2ea44f)
![Flutter](https://img.shields.io/badge/Frontend-Flutter-02569B)
![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Backend-Go-00ADD8)

<img src="flutter_ui/android/app/src/main/res/drawable/banner.png" alt="iTaK Gaming TV banner">

</div>

**Plan:** [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) · **Tasks:** [TODO.md](TODO.md) · **Ideas:** [IDEA.md](IDEA.md) · **Build rules:** [docs/RULES.md](docs/RULES.md)

## What it is

iTaK Gaming is a family arcade emulator built by a disabled veteran for his family, and open source so other families can use it too. It has no accounts and no RetroArch dependency. The Flutter frontend is built for a TV remote first, and the Go backend runs emulator cores directly.

Players keep separate profiles and save states. The app checks for its own updates, and online play uses public lobbies while both sides run the same game locally.

## What works today

- Flutter TV frontend with system select, game grid, player profiles, online lobbies, leaderboard, settings, logs, avatars, and update offers
- Go emulator host with core-negotiated pixel formats, correct aspect handling, audio capture, controller input, and per-player save states
- Clean-room Go core modules under `cores/` for the bundled system families
- Public lobby netplay with open or password lobbies, spectators, friends, play stats, and leaderboards
- Lockstep online play: only inputs and signals cross the network, never a streamed game
- Self-update checks with SHA-256 verification before the installer opens
- Headless backend and core test harnesses

## Quickstart

Try the backend:

```bash
cd go_backend
go build ./...
go run ./cmd
curl http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/systems
```

Run the lobby server:

```bash
cd netplay
go run ./cmd/lobbyserver
go test ./...
```

Headless core tests need a core and a legally obtained game or test program supplied by the developer. See each core README under `cores/` for its proof status and limits.

## The grid: module map

| Module | What it owns |
| :--- | :--- |
| `flutter_ui/` | TV-first frontend: menus, game grid, profiles, online room, leaderboard, settings, logs, updates |
| `go_backend/` | Emulator host: core bridge, video, audio, input, saves, local API, mobile binding, test tools |
| `cores/go-*` | One clean-room Go core module per system, with tests beside each chip and subsystem |
| `netplay/` | Lobby server, WebSocket signaling, spectators, friends, stats, leaderboards, app distribution |
| `MISSOURI-KIT.md` | Family setup and recovery instructions for the Missouri box |
| `SPECTATOR_DESIGN.md` | Spectator and big-lobby design |
| `VOICE_CHAT_RESEARCH.md` | Voice chat research and the limits of TV microphones |

## Platform builds

| Build | Targets | Systems |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Android 32-bit | Chromecast HD | The lighter system set that fits the stick |
| Android 64-bit | Google TV Streamer, Shield, stronger TV boxes | The wider system set |
| Windows 64-bit | PC | All supported systems |
| Linux 64-bit | PC and repurposed boxes | All supported systems |

Builds are separate on purpose. A weak TV stick does not carry systems it cannot run well.

## ROMs, firmware, and cores

This repo ships **no ROMs and no core binaries**. Both are excluded by `.gitignore`.

- Games: use your own legally obtained backups.
- Firmware or BIOS files: supply your own where a system needs one.
- Cores: the source tree carries the project's Go core modules; external libretro cores, where still used by a build, remain separate projects with their own licenses.

Saves live under `saves/<player>/<game>/slot<N>.sav`, with 10 slots per player per game. Switching players switches save sets.

## Status

iTaK Gaming 1.62, build 63, was published to the update feed and its public APK hash was verified on 2026-10-17. The detailed proof and remaining work live in [TODO.md](TODO.md). A build is not called ready here until the shipped app has been run on the target device and a game has launched.

## License

MIT for the code in this repository; see [LICENSE](LICENSE). External cores and libraries keep their own licenses. Respect the license manifest for the exact build before adding any revenue feature.

==================== FILE: SETTINGS_FOCUS_FIX.md ====================

# Settings screen: D-pad focus fix + popup rework (candidate, not shipped)

Tree: ~/itak-scratch-settingsfix (copy of the 1.105 app tree).
Changed files: flutter_ui/lib/main.dart (Settings screen + a new
_LogsPopup class), flutter_ui/android/.../MainActivity.kt (one new
channel case), flutter_ui/test/settings_screen_test.dart (new tests).
Nothing pushed, published, or staged. No TV contact.

## The bug (owner, on 1.105)

In Settings, pressing UP deep in the list threw focus to the circular
back arrow at the top-left of the header band. RIGHT rescued it once,
UP then moved exactly one row, and focus escaped to the back button
again. Vertical navigation inside the list was effectively broken.

## Root cause

SettingsScreen (main.dart) was the only menu screen still using a
manual-cursor design:

- The 13 rows were plain GestureDetector + AnimatedContainer cards.
  None of them was a focusable widget; the highlight was just an int
  (_row) driving a border color.
- The only focus node in the body was one KeyboardListener node
  (_focusNode) whose render box spans the whole body. Its handler
  (_onKey) updated _row on arrow keys -- but KeyboardListener always
  returns KeyEventResult.ignored, so the framework's default
  directional focus traversal ALSO processed every arrow press,
  geometrically, against the only two traversal targets in the route:
  that body-wide node and the AppBar's BackButton (a focusable
  IconButton in the header band, left of the "Settings" title).
- UP from the body-wide rect: the one node above its top edge is the
  BackButton, so real focus jumped there (the highlight moved once via
  _onKey on the same press, which is why it looked like it half
  worked). The BackButton lives in the AppBar subtree, NOT under the
  KeyboardListener, so from then on _onKey never fired again and the
  remote was dead.
- Owner's workaround, decoded: RIGHT from the BackButton traversed
  back into the body-wide node ("somewhere inside the row"), the next
  UP fired _onKey once (one row) AND re-triggered traversal straight
  back to the BackButton. Exactly the reported behavior.
- DOWN mostly survived because nothing focusable sits below the body
  rect, so traversal found no candidate and focus stayed put.

Screens that navigate fine (home grid, game lists, Manage players,
Who's playing) use real per-item focusables (InkWell/Focus with
onFocusChange, 1.98 restructure): every item owns a node with its own
rect, so traversal steps item to item. LogScreen likewise returns
KeyEventResult from a real Focus handler. Settings now follows the
same pattern.

## The fix (focus)

- 13 FocusNodes (_rowFocus, debug labels settings-row-0..12), one per
  row, via a _focusableRow(index, child) wrapper (Focus +
  onFocusChange). When focus lands on a row, _row follows it and
  _ensureRowVisible scrolls it into view: highlight and focus are the
  same thing by construction.
- _onKey no longer handles UP/DOWN (traversal owns them) and no
  longer cycles values on LEFT/RIGHT. It only activates the focused
  row on enter/select/space.
- _focusNode.skipTraversal = true, and focus starts on row 0's node:
  the body-wide listener node can never be a traversal target again,
  but still receives key events as an ancestor of the focused row.
- Resulting geometry: UP/DOWN step card to card through the whole
  list and stop at the ends (the old modulo wrap-around is gone,
  matching the rest of the app). UP from row 0 reaches the header
  back button deliberately; DOWN from it returns to row 0.

## The popup rework (owner: rows pop up like a box, AlphaFlux style)

Activation (CENTER or tap) on a row opens an AlertDialog in the app's
established popup style (showDialog, barrier black 0.8, card
0xFF262640, green 0xFF00E676 affirmative, BACK closes), with a default
choice autofocused. Closing any popup returns focus to the
originating row (_activateRow -> _restoreRowFocus).

- Toggle rows (0 Swap, 1 Box art, 2 Auto-save, 3 Friend alerts,
  7 Space background, 8 Intro video, 9 Debug reports): popup titled
  with the row label, content "Now: On/Off", actions Off / On with
  the current value green + bold and autofocused; picking applies
  state + pref (same writes the old _adjust made) and closes.
- Sound test (4): popup carrying the DEBUG card from the native
  SoundTestActivity: "Measure sound delay" button + readout text,
  "Send debug report now" button + status text. The measurement runs
  through ONE new channel case, "measureSoundDelay" in
  MainActivity.kt, whose body is the same algorithm and result
  wording as SoundTestActivity.measureDelay (EmuAudioOutput track,
  220 Hz tone, AudioTimestamp median), minus its UI posts; it runs
  ~3 s on a worker thread. The report button uses the Dart
  DebugChute.sendReport (immediate send with a real sent/failed
  result in the popup). The speaker/mic level-bar tests are NOT in
  the popup; SoundTestActivity still exists in the APK but Settings
  no longer launches it (the Dart 'soundTest' call is gone).
- App updates (5): popup shows the installed build and a "Check for
  updates" button; the button closes the popup and runs the
  pre-existing _openUpdates flow byte-for-byte (its own up-to-date /
  offer / failure dialogs unchanged).
- Logs (6): _LogsPopup, a scrollable popup box (780x420) fed by the
  same readLog channel as LogScreen, opening scrolled to the bottom,
  with Page up / Page down (+-320, same step as LogScreen), Refresh,
  and Close (autofocused). LogScreen itself is untouched and still in
  the tree.
- Send report (10): one popup runs the whole flow in place: the
  Debug-reports-off gate message (same words), else confirm (Send
  autofocused) -> "Sending..." -> "Report sent" / "Report failed"
  with the same result strings the old dialogs used.
- Install code (11): read-only popup showing the FULL install code
  (the row keeps its 8-character short form).
- Back (12): plain exit row, no popup, unchanged.

==================== FILE: SOUND_TEST_NOTES.md ====================

# Sound test screen: notes for the wiring step

The screen itself is done: `SoundTestActivity` lives in
`flutter_ui/android/app/src/main/kotlin/net/itak/itak_gaming/SoundTestActivity.kt`
and is registered in `AndroidManifest.xml` as `.SoundTestActivity`,
exported false, landscape, fullscreen theme, label "Sound test".
What remains is one launch hook from Settings, which is a separate
step because it touches MainActivity and main.dart.

## Proposed launch contract

No extras, no arguments, no return value. Either of these works:

1. Preferred, matches how the rest of the app talks to native
   code: add one case to the existing MethodChannel handler in
   MainActivity (channel name `net.itak/emu`), like this:

   - Method name: `soundTest`
   - Handler body: `startActivity(Intent(this, SoundTestActivity::class.java))`,
     then `result.success(null)`.
   - Dart side, later, from the Settings screen:
     `MethodChannel('net.itak/emu').invokeMethod('soundTest')`.

2. Or any Kotlin code inside the app can launch it directly with
   an intent to `net.itak.itak_gaming.SoundTestActivity`. The
   fully qualified class name is
   `net.itak.itak_gaming.SoundTestActivity`.

BACK inside the screen finishes the activity, so the caller needs
no result handling.

## Mic input fallback order (as implemented)

AudioRecord configurations are tried in this order, and the first
one that both initializes and reaches the recording state wins:

1. Source VOICE_RECOGNITION at 44100 Hz
2. Source VOICE_RECOGNITION at 16000 Hz
3. Source MIC at 44100 Hz
4. Source MIC at 16000 Hz

All attempts are mono, PCM 16 bit, with a buffer of the larger of
the platform minimum and 4096 bytes.

The builder never pins a specific device, so recording goes to
the system default input. A USB microphone plugged into the box
becomes that default and is picked up automatically. Bluetooth
SCO is deliberately not forced: a box that exposes a Bluetooth
mic as a normal input device will use it, and a box that does
not will honestly report that no microphone was found, which is
exactly what this screen exists to find out before voice chat
depends on it.

## Speaker path

The jingle is generated PCM, no audio assets: three rising notes
at 440, 554.37 and 659.25 Hz, 0.60 seconds each with 0.08 second
gaps (1.96 seconds total), stereo, peak level 0.62 of full scale.
The AudioTrack uses USAGE_GAME so the test exercises the same
audio path the emulator uses, and a fixed track volume.

## Meter math

- Speaker bar target: the peak absolute sample value of the
  generated chunk most recently written to the AudioTrack,
  divided by 32767.
- Mic bar target: the peak absolute sample value of the most
  recent AudioRecord buffer, divided by 32768.
- Peak percent label: the loudest mic buffer peak seen since the
  test started, as peak times 100 divided by 32768.
- Display easing runs on a 40 ms ticker: the shown level closes
  55 percent of the gap when rising and multiplies by 0.86 when
  falling, so bars punch up fast and settle to zero instead of
  snapping off.

## Permission note

`RECORD_AUDIO` was added to the manifest alongside the activity
entry. Without the declaration the runtime request from the
screen would be denied instantly with no dialog, and the mic
test could never run. The screen still handles denial itself:
it asks with the standard requestPermissions flow and, on
denial, shows plain text saying the box cannot hear you.


==================== FILE: SPECTATOR_DESIGN.md ====================

# Spectator and big-lobby design (David's arcade room vision, 2026-10-12)

Goal: a lobby stops being two people. Two player seats, a crowd of
spectators, a host who runs the seats, a Got Next line, and later
host-run tournaments with their own leaderboard. This doc is the
skeleton those builds follow.

## What the current code already gives us

- The signaling hub (netplay/internal/server/hub.go) keeps a SET of
  sockets per lobby with no size cap and relays every client message
  verbatim to everyone else in the room. Fan-out to spectators is
  free; nothing in the transport assumes two peers.
- Peers already carry a lobby.Role (host, guest). Spectator is a
  third role, not a new concept.
- The 2-player limit lives in the lobby membership layer
  (internal/lobby, MaxPlayers) and in the client session
  (internal/netsession assumes exactly one peer). Those are the two
  places the work lands.
- Lockstep means a spectator does not need video. It runs the same
  core and ROM locally and applies both players' input streams,
  GGPO style. Input frames are tiny, so ten spectators cost the
  players almost nothing.
- Chat already relays room-wide. Spectators read and send chat with
  no protocol change.

## Protocol changes (all backward compatible)

Old clients ignore unknown JSON fields, and the relay is verbatim,
so every change below is additive. A session_offer gains "v": 2;
a v1 peer answers session_reject and the host falls back politely.

1. Seat-tagged inputs. The input envelope gains "seat": 1 or 2,
   set by the sender. Two-player games read it as "the peer's seat"
   exactly as today (the peer is always the other seat). A watcher
   needs the tag to know which stream is player 1 and which is
   player 2.
2. Roster notices. The server already mints lifecycle notices
   (peer_joined, peer_left). It gains "roster": the full member
   list [{name, role, seat}] sent to the room on every membership
   change, so every client (players and watchers) sees the same
   room: who holds the seats, who is watching, who is in line.
3. Watch join. POST /lobbies/{id}/watch {player, password?} issues
   a spectator token (cap: 10 spectators per lobby, host can close
   watching by making the lobby private as today). The listing
   payload gains a spectators count.
4. Mid-match sync for watchers. A watcher sends "watch_sync"; the
   host answers with the existing snapshot resync payload (state at
   frame F). The watcher loads the snapshot, then applies seat
   tagged inputs from F onward. Same machinery as desync recovery,
   pointed at a third client.
5. Back to room. A game ending today ends the session. Rotation
   needs "match_end": both players return to the room phase on the
   same sockets (like peer_left in the room phase, voluntary and
   mutual), the lobby persists, and a new match can start with
   different seat holders. Either player can send it; the host's
   client treats its own send as authoritative for rotation.

## Who referees what

- The host client is the referee for v1: seat assignment, swaps,
  random pick-two, and the Got Next line all live in host-side
  envelopes ("seat_assign" {seat, player}, "got_next" join/leave
  broadcasts, queue order replicated from roster plus queue
  messages). No server state, no new persistence. If the host
  leaves, the room ends, which is acceptable for v1 and matches
  today's host-leaves rule.
- Match results for the tournament board are reported by the host
  client (POST /matches {game, p1, p2, winner, lobby}) into a
  stats-style store. Honor system, stated plainly in the UI. A
  server-refereed queue is the tournament-grade upgrade if abuse
  ever shows up; it is not needed for family and streamer rooms.

## Build slices

- S1 server: spectator role + watch join + roster notices + listing
  counts, with tests. Deploy as the next lobby image.
- S2 netsession: seat-tagged inputs, watch mode (never sends input,
  ready, or countdown; applies both streams; watch_sync snapshot
  join), match_end phase return. Race-tested like the rest of the
  package.
- S3 Android: waiting room member list (seats, watchers, queue),
  watch screen (emulator view, inputs locked, chat available),
  join-as-spectator entry from the lobby list and Friends.
- S4 host controls: seat assign and swap UI, random pick-two,
  between-match flow on match_end.
- S5 Got Next: queue join from the watch screen, auto-promotion of
  the line head into the loser's seat on match_end, winner stays.
- S6 tournaments: match reporting, tournament store and board,
  host tournament setup (game, best-of, bracket from the room).

## Risks and open points

- Password lobbies: spectators need the password too. Same secret,
  no separate watcher password in v1.
- A watcher on a slow box falls behind the input stream; the
  snapshot resync is also the catch-up mechanism (request a fresh
  watch_sync when more than a few seconds behind).
- Voice chat with spectators: v1 voice stays between the two seat
  holders. Room-wide voice is a mixer problem and waits.
- The public lobby payload exposes only hostPlayer today, which is
  why a friend guesting in someone else's lobby is not joinable
  from the Friends list. S1's roster work fixes that as a side
  effect (guest name becomes visible server-side).

==================== FILE: VOICE_CHAT_RESEARCH.md ====================

# Voice Chat Research Spike

Date: 2026-10-12. Status: research only, no code written.
Scope: two player voice chat during netplay (waiting room and in game),
building on the text chat that already shipped.

## How our stack constrains this (read first)

Facts from our own tree, because they decide most of the design:

* The lobby server relays JSON envelopes verbatim between the two
  players and never parses them (netplay/PROTOCOL.md section 3).
  Section 3.1 already reserves `{"type":"offer"}`, `{"type":"answer"}`
  and `{"type":"ice"}` envelopes over that socket, with the guest as
  offerer and the host as answerer. Envelope cap is 256 KB; an SDP
  body is a few KB, so size is a non issue.
* The WebSocket is owned by Go. `netsession.reader()` in
  go_backend/internal/netsession/step.go unmarshals every envelope
  and dispatches on `type`; unknown types are dropped. Kotlin never
  touches the socket.
* Text chat already proved the pattern for Kotlin facing session
  data: go_backend/internal/netsession/chat.go stores messages in
  the session, and go_backend/mobile/netplay.go exposes
  `NetplaySendChat` plus `NetplayChatJSON(afterSeq)` over the
  gomobile bridge. EmulatorActivity polls that JSON from its room
  ticker and chat ticker and renders programmatic views.
* Game audio is ours, not the system's: EmulatorActivity.startAudio()
  builds an AudioTrack with USAGE_GAME and CONTENT_TYPE_MUSIC and
  feeds it from `Mobile.drainAudio()` on the game loop thread.
* The app builds armeabi-v7a only (abiFilters in
  flutter_ui/android/app/build.gradle, for the Chromecast HD) with
  minSdk 24. Any native library we add must ship a 32 bit ARM build.
* Repositories are already google() plus mavenCentral() in
  flutter_ui/android/build.gradle. Nothing else is configured.
* The manifest has no RECORD_AUDIO permission today.
* Remote keys today (EmulatorActivity.mapButtonRaw): DPAD_CENTER and
  ENTER are ButtonB, KEYCODE_ASSIST and KEYCODE_VOICE_ASSIST are
  ButtonA, MEDIA_PLAY_PAUSE is Start, and the gamepad thumb stick
  clicks (KEYCODE_BUTTON_THUMB_L / THUMB_R) are not mapped at all.

## 1. The WebRTC library

### Google's own artifact is a dead end

`org.webrtc:google-webrtc` stopped at version 1.0.32006 in August
2020. It was only ever published to Google's Bintray repo and
JCenter, both shut down years ago, so it does not resolve from
google() or mavenCentral() in a fresh Gradle build today. Anyone
still referencing it is pinned to a 2020 WebRTC with six years of
unpatched media stack bugs. Do not use it.

Source: https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.webrtc/google-webrtc/1.0.32006
(artifact record shows the Bintray repo and the Aug 2020 date).

### Use io.github.webrtc-sdk:android from Maven Central

The maintained successor is the webrtc-sdk community build:

* Coordinates: `io.github.webrtc-sdk:android`, published on Maven
  Central, so our existing mavenCentral() resolves it with no repo
  changes. Current builds track upstream WebRTC milestones (POMs
  and the project README show the 144 and 150 milestone lines;
  pin the newest at build time).
* License: BSD 3-Clause, stated in the Maven POM. That is the
  upstream WebRTC license, permissive, fine next to our MIT repo.
  One catch found in a third party audit of the AAR: the AAR itself
  contains no license or notice file, so we should ship the WebRTC
  BSD notice in our own notices file when we redistribute the APK.
* Contents: the AAR bundles native libs for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a,
  x86 and x86_64, and declares minSdk 21. The armeabi-v7a slice is
  roughly 7 MB uncompressed; because our build already sets
  abiFilters to armeabi-v7a, only that slice lands in the APK.
* API compatibility: it keeps the upstream `org.webrtc` package, so
  all upstream API documentation and examples apply unchanged.

Sources:
https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.webrtc-sdk/android
https://github.com/webrtc-sdk/android/blob/HEAD/README.md
https://github.com/shady-2096/meo-mic/blob/HEAD/adr/0008-android-webrtc-distribution.md
(AAR contents, ARMv7 size, minSdk and license findings.)

### Alternatives, briefly

* `org.jitsi:webrtc`: Jitsi's builds of the same upstream code, also
  on Maven Central, kept current for Jitsi Meet. A credible fallback
  if the webrtc-sdk line ever stalls.
* Building libwebrtc from source: always possible, always a last
  resort. Hours of depot_tools and GN work per milestone and a big
  burden on the build server. Not justified for audio only.
* Signal's `org.whispersystems:webrtc-android` is ancient (M77) and
  GPLv3. Reject on both counts.

## 2. Audio only PeerConnection in Kotlin, and where signaling lives

### Minimal shape

One small Kotlin class (call it VoiceChat.kt) next to
EmulatorActivity, roughly:

1. One time init: `PeerConnectionFactory.initialize(...)` with
   default options, then build the factory with a
   `JavaAudioDeviceModule` (see section 3 for its settings) and no
   video factories at all. Audio only means no EGL, no capturers,
   no surface views.
2. ICE config: one STUN server entry (section 4), no TURN in v1.
3. `factory.createPeerConnection(rtcConfig, observer)` with a
   single local audio track:
   `createAudioSource(MediaConstraints())` then
   `createAudioTrack("voice", source)`, added with `addTrack`.
   Incoming audio needs no code beyond the track existing;
   libwebrtc plays remote audio through the audio device module
   automatically.
4. Offer and answer: the guest creates the offer
   (`pc.createOffer` then `setLocalDescription`), serializes
   `{"type":"offer","sdp":...}` and hands it to the bridge. The host
   sets it as remote description, creates the answer, and replies
   with `{"type":"answer","sdp":...}`. This is exactly the exchange
   PROTOCOL.md 3.1 already describes, roles included, which also
   removes any glare question: only the guest ever offers.
5. ICE trickle: `onIceCandidate` in Kotlin serializes each candidate
   into `{"type":"ice","candidate":...,"sdpMid":...,"sdpMLineIndex":...}`;
   the reverse path calls `pc.addIceCandidate`. Buffer incoming
   candidates until the remote description is set.
6. Mute and push to talk are one call: `audioTrack.setEnabled(...)`.
   No renegotiation needed.

Signaling messages are tiny and infrequent (one offer, one answer,
a burst of ICE candidates in the first second). A polling bridge at
the cadence the room and chat tickers already use is plenty fast;
nothing here needs sub second delivery beyond what chat already
tolerates.

### Recommendation: signaling rides through Go, media stays in Kotlin

Put a `signal.go` in internal/netsession that is a deliberate copy
of chat.go's shape: the reader switch gains cases for `offer`,
`answer` and `ice` that append the raw payloads to a small capped
queue; `Session.SendSignal(rawJSON)` writes an envelope out;
`SignalSince(afterSeq)` drains it with the same cursor pattern as
`ChatSince`. The gomobile bridge gains `NetplaySendSignal(json)` and
`NetplaySignalJSON(afterSeq)`, mirroring the chat pair one for one.
Kotlin polls, parses each payload, and feeds the PeerConnection.
Voice starts when the waiting room forms (so players can talk
before Ready, like the text chat) and stays up for the whole
session; the envelopes ride the same socket before, during and
after the lockstep game because the socket outlives every phase.

Why not let Kotlin open its own second WebSocket to the lobby
server and keep Go out of it: the server caps concurrent sockets
per IP (10), the token and lobby lifecycle already live in the Go
session, a second socket can die or be reaped independently of the
game, and we would maintain two connection states for one room.
The Go queue costs a few dozen lines and reuses a proven shape.

### Echo cancellation and processing defaults

libwebrtc's built in audio processing (AEC3 echo canceller, noise
suppression, automatic gain control) runs on the capture path by
default; it is not something we have to switch on. On top of that
the JavaAudioDeviceModule builder offers
`setUseHardwareAcousticEchoCanceler` and
`setUseHardwareNoiseSuppressor`, which engage the device's own
effects when the audio HAL advertises them, and
`setAudioSource(...)`, where MediaRecorder.AudioSource
.VOICE_COMMUNICATION is the right pick because Android attaches
its voice path processing to that source. Recommendation: ship the
defaults first (VOICE_COMMUNICATION source, hardware effects
allowed). The builder flags exist because some device HALs ship
broken hardware AEC; if the Chromecast or a future box misbehaves,
flipping those two flags to false forces the software path, which
is the known workaround in the field.
## 3. Microphones on Android TV: the honest picture

### The remote control mic is not available to us

This is the finding that shapes the feature. On Google TV devices
like our Chromecast HD, the Voice Remote's microphone streams over
Bluetooth to the system's voice interaction service. Google's own
support docs describe the button purely as the Assistant trigger:
press and hold the microphone button and Google Assistant listens.
The remote mic does not appear as an audio input device that apps
can enumerate, and no AudioSource value selects it. Third party
projects that capture this remote's audio do it by talking to the
remote's Bluetooth protocol directly from another computer, which
tells you where the audio actually terminates: the system voice
service, not the app audio stack.

Our own activity does receive KEYCODE_ASSIST and KEYCODE_VOICE_ASSIST
key events on our box (they are mapped to ButtonA today), so the
press reaches us. The audio does not. Plan on the remote mic being
Assistant only; voice chat needs a real audio input device.

Sources:
https://support.google.com/chromecast/answer/7582438?hl=en
https://github.com/kaliscuit/remotebuddy/blob/HEAD/README.en.md

### USB microphone: the reliable v1 input

A USB Audio Class mic or headset dongle plugged into the TV (on
the Chromecast, through the usual powered USB hub) enumerates as a
normal input device (AudioDeviceInfo TYPE_USB_HEADSET or
TYPE_USB_DEVICE) and standard capture works once RECORD_AUDIO is
granted. WebRTC's audio module records from the system default
communication input, which a plugged in USB mic normally becomes.
Two cautions: enumerate inputs at runtime and show the chosen
input's name in the voice settings, so "no mic found" is a visible
state rather than silent failure; and TV class hardware varies
(at least one popular TV box line has a broken USB audio HAL), so
verify on the actual Death Star Chromecast before promising
anything. That verification is step zero of the build.

### Bluetooth headset (SCO): best effort only

TV boxes pair Bluetooth headsets for output (A2DP) readily. The
microphone half needs the SCO / HFP input path, and support on
Android TV devices is inconsistent to absent; many boxes simply
never expose a TYPE_BLUETOOTH_SCO input. If one appears, the
standard capture path picks it up with no special code. Treat it
as a pleasant surprise, never a v1 dependency.

### RECORD_AUDIO permission flow on TV

RECORD_AUDIO is a runtime (dangerous) permission. The request
dialog works on Android TV and is D-pad navigable; there is no
missing permission UI problem on stock Google TV. Rules for us:

* Declare the permission in the manifest (it is absent today), and
  mark the microphone feature not required
  (`android.hardware.microphone` required false) so the app keeps
  installing on mic less boxes, consistent with how the manifest
  already treats touchscreen and leanback.
* Ask lazily, the first time the player turns voice on in the
  waiting room or settings, never at app start. Denial degrades to
  text chat plus listening, with one line of explanation.
* Capture only ever runs while EmulatorActivity is in the
  foreground inside a session, so Android's background microphone
  restrictions (no capture from background apps on modern Android)
  never come into play. Expect the system mic indicator while
  voice is live; that is correct behavior, not a bug.

### Mixing voice with game audio, and the echo question

No manual mixing is needed. Game audio keeps its own AudioTrack
(USAGE_GAME). WebRTC plays the partner's voice through its audio
device module's own track (voice communication attributes) and
AudioFlinger mixes the two streams. Volume keys keep controlling
the TV as today.

Two real interactions to watch:

* The Java audio module puts the device into MODE_IN_COMMUNICATION
  while voice runs. On a TV there is no earpiece to misroute to,
  so this is mostly harmless, but if a Bluetooth SCO device is
  connected it can try to pull all audio toward the headset. The
  module builder accepts custom AudioAttributes for its playout,
  which is the lever if routing misbehaves on real hardware.
* Echo: WebRTC's echo canceller uses its own rendered signal (the
  partner's voice) as its reference. Our game audio is rendered by
  a different track, so the canceller does not know it exists and
  cannot subtract it. Game sound coming out of TV speakers will
  reach a room mic as ordinary background sound. Noise suppression
  dulls it; it does not remove it. The practical defenses are the
  ones speakerphone users have always had: a mic near the player
  (USB mic or headset) instead of across the room, reasonable TV
  volume, and push to talk (section 5). This is the strongest
  argument for making push to talk the default.

## 4. NAT: STUN first, TURN only on evidence

Recommendation: agree with the staged plan. Ship v1 with STUN
only (public STUN, for example Google's stun.l.google.com:19302),
log the ICE connection state and the winning candidate pair type
on both boxes, and run the real Kentucky to Missouri test. Add
TURN only if that test actually fails.

Why this is the right order:

* Both endpoints are ordinary home broadband routers, one per
  household, each player directly on their home network. Consumer
  NAT is overwhelmingly cone style (full, restricted or port
  restricted), and ICE connects cone to cone through server
  reflexive candidates alone. Symmetric NAT, the kind that defeats
  STUN, is mostly a carrier grade NAT and enterprise firewall
  phenomenon, not a home router one.
* Voice is the most forgiving WebRTC workload: one low bitrate
  Opus stream, no video, tolerant of the extra milliseconds a
  relay would add anyway.
* Skipping TURN keeps v1 free of new server surface. TURN is not
  just a package install; it is a public relay that needs
  credential hygiene and abuse limits (below).
* The failure, if it exists, is cheap to detect: ICE state goes to
  failed or stays disconnected on one or both boxes, and the
  candidate log shows no srflx pair. We will know in one session
  whether these two specific households need a relay, instead of
  guessing for households in general.

The TURN fallback, scoped so it can be added in an evening:
coturn on the same Ubuntu server that hosts the lobby. Install via
apt (`apt install coturn`) or the official coturn/coturn Docker
image with host networking (TURN needs its full UDP relay range,
which is why host networking is the norm). Ports: 3478 UDP and TCP
for STUN and TURN, 5349 for TURN over TLS if wanted, and the relay
range 49152 to 65535 UDP, which for two households can be pinned
much narrower with min-port and max-port. Credentials: use the
time limited model, coturn's `use-auth-secret` with a
`static-auth-secret`; the lobby server mints usernames of the form
expiry:player with an HMAC-SHA1 password, valid for hours, so no
long lived password ever ships inside the app. Lock it down with
quotas and denied-peer-ip ranges for private networks, because an
open TURN server on the public internet gets found and abused as
free bandwidth. The clients then get one extra iceServers entry
with those minted credentials, delivered through the lobby exactly
like other session setup data. If even TURN failed (it would mean
UDP is blocked outright on one side), the last resort is relaying
voice over the lobby WebSocket itself; that is a server change and
explicitly out of scope unless reality demands it.

## 5. Push to talk: which buttons actually exist

Constraints from our own key map and from Android TV behavior:

* The remote's mic button sends KEYCODE_ASSIST / KEYCODE_VOICE_ASSIST.
  On our box the key event does reach the activity (it is ButtonA
  today). But holding it is the system gesture for summoning the
  Assistant, OEM behavior varies, and the same key is a gameplay
  button (A). Using it as hold to talk would fight the Assistant,
  fire A in game, and behave differently on the Missouri box if its
  remote differs. Not viable as the primary.
* KEYCODE_VOICE_INPUT exists on some remotes but is delivered even
  less consistently than ASSIST. Same verdict.
* Every face button, shoulder and the D-pad are gameplay inputs in
  the 16 button mask; stealing one breaks games that use the full
  pad.
* The gamepad stick clicks, KEYCODE_BUTTON_THUMB_L (L3) and
  KEYCODE_BUTTON_THUMB_R (R3), are the exception: mapButtonRaw does
  not map them at all, libretro cores in our set do not consume
  them, and a stick click is holdable for minutes without
  interfering with play.

Recommended scheme:

* Default: push to talk, hold R3 on a gamepad (L3 accepted too).
  Implemented at the existing onKeyDown / onKeyUp choke point:
  when voice is on, THUMB_R down calls setEnabled(true) on the
  audio track, up calls setEnabled(false). Latency is a non issue
  because the track and connection stay live; only the gate moves.
* Remote only players (no gamepad): a voice mode setting with
  three values: Push to talk (R3), Toggle (tap the remote mic /
  ASSIST key once to open the mic, tap again to close; a tap is a
  key event we already receive, and a tap does not summon the
  Assistant the way a hold does), and Open mic.
* Open mic offered for headset and USB mic users who want it, off
  by default, because of the echo picture in section 3.
* A mute state indicator lives in the waiting room and pause menu
  (Mic live / Mic muted / No mic found), plus a brief on screen
  flash when the mic opens in game, so nobody guesses whether they
  are transmitting.

## 6. Effort estimate and top risks

Rough sizes, in the order we would build them:

* Step zero hardware check (S): enumerate audio inputs on the
  Death Star with a USB mic attached; confirm capture works before
  any WebRTC code. Half a day including the write up.
* Gradle plus manifest (S): one dependency line
  (io.github.webrtc-sdk:android), RECORD_AUDIO, microphone feature
  not required. An hour, plus one pipeline build to prove the
  server resolves Maven Central and the v7a slice links. Note:
  release builds are not minified today; if minify is ever
  enabled, add the standard org.webrtc keep rules.
* Go signaling queue (S): signal.go beside chat.go (about 120
  lines), three reader cases, two bridge functions in
  mobile/netplay.go, plus unit tests mirroring the chat tests.
  Well under a day.
* Kotlin VoiceChat module (L): the real work. Factory and audio
  module setup, one PeerConnection, offer / answer / ICE glue to
  the bridge, connection state reporting, teardown tied to
  session end. About 400 to 600 lines, two to three days
  including on device debugging.
* UI surfaces (M): waiting room voice status row, mic request
  prompt, input device name. Pause menu voice entry with mode and
  mute state. Settings (Dart side prefs read by Kotlin, the
  established pattern): voice on or off, mode (PTT / toggle /
  open), read by the activity at session start. One to two days
  across Kotlin and Dart.
* NAT field test (S): one real Kentucky to Missouri session with
  ICE logging on both ends. The coturn fallback, only if
  triggered, is about half a day of server work plus a small
  lobby server addition to mint credentials.

Top three risks:

1. Input hardware reality. The remote mic is Assistant only, so
   voice chat silently depends on each household having a USB mic
   or a headset the box can hear. If the Missouri box has neither,
   the feature ships to an audience of one. This is why the
   hardware check is step zero, not a launch day surprise.
2. Audio path fights on cheap TV hardware. Broken or absent
   hardware echo cancellation, MODE_IN_COMMUNICATION rerouting
   surprises, and game audio bleed into a room mic can make voice
   sound bad in ways no amount of signaling code fixes. Push to
   talk by default and the builder flags for forcing software
   processing are the mitigations; both are planned, neither is
   proven on our box yet.
3. One of the two households has hostile NAT after all (double
   NAT, an ISP router doing symmetric NAT, or UDP filtering).
   Probability is low, impact is total for that pair, and the
   fix (coturn) is scoped and costed above. We accept the risk
   knowingly by testing the real pair early.

## Recommended v1 scope

1. Kotlin VoiceChat module on io.github.webrtc-sdk:android (Maven Central, BSD 3-Clause), audio only, one PeerConnection per session.
2. Signaling through Go: signal.go modeled on chat.go, bridge pair NetplaySendSignal / NetplaySignalJSON; guest offers, host answers, per PROTOCOL.md 3.1.
3. Voice lives from waiting room formation to session end; text chat untouched.
4. Input: USB mic as the supported path, input enumerated at runtime and named in settings; Bluetooth SCO only if the box exposes it; remote mic documented as Assistant only.
5. RECORD_AUDIO requested lazily on first voice enable; denial degrades to listen plus text.
6. Push to talk by default (hold R3 or L3), ASSIST tap toggles for remote only players, open mic as a setting; mic state shown in waiting room and pause menu.
7. STUN only (public STUN), with ICE state and candidate logging on both boxes from day one.
8. Ship gate: the real Kentucky to Missouri session. coturn on the Ubuntu server is pre scoped as the immediate follow up if, and only if, that test fails.

==================== FILE: cores/go-dreamcast/README.md ====================

# go-dreamcast

A from-scratch Sega Dreamcast core in pure Go, part of iTaK Gaming.
MIT licensed. Users supply their own game images; this repository
contains no game data, no Dreamcast BIOS or firmware bytes, and no
dumped code of any kind.

## DC-1: what is in this slice

* `chips/sh4`: the SH-4 CPU. Integer pipeline, the FPU (single and
  double precision, FPU register banks, FPSCR modes), and a
  functional MMU: UTLB translation with page sizes, protection
  checks and the P1, P2, P3, P4 and store queue areas. With the
  MMU off, addresses are masked to their 29-bit physical form.
* `bus`: the physical memory map (below). Multi-byte accesses are
  composed little-endian from bytes, so unaligned accesses work at
  the bus level.
* `gd`: GD-ROM image reading for `.gdi`, `.iso` and `.bin` files,
  with ISO9660 directory walking and IP.BIN parsing (the bootstrap
  header every Dreamcast disc carries: title, product number,
  region, peripherals and the boot file name).
* `system`: the machine skeleton. It wires CPU, bus and disc
  together, runs frames on a flat cycle budget, holds controller
  state, and implements save states.

## DC-2: what is in this slice

Real interrupt delivery, the SPG display timing generator, and
the PowerVR2 tile renderer.

* `chips/sh4` interrupt model: `RaiseInterrupt` now latches a
  pending request (highest level wins) instead of vectoring
  immediately. Acceptance at the instruction boundary honors
  SR.BL and SR.IMASK (the level must exceed the mask), wakes a
  halted CPU, sets INTEVT at acceptance time, and can be
  withdrawn before acceptance. Exceptions keep their immediate
  behavior.
* `holly`: the Holly system interrupt block at 0x005F6900.
  SB_ISTNRM (write-1-to-clear), SB_ISTEXT (device-clear only),
  SB_ISTERR (write-1-to-clear), and the IML2LVL, IML4LVL,
  IML6LVL mask rows (per bank). Reads of ISTNRM carry bit 30
  when any external source is pending and bit 31 when any
  error source is pending. The highest masked level wins and
  is presented to the CPU with INTEVT 0x320 at level 6, 0x360
  at level 4, 0x3A0 at level 2, following the published ASIC
  event table: event ids are the ISTNRM bit indices (render
  done video 0, ISP 1, TSP 2, vblank in 3, vblank out 4,
  hblank 5, YUV done 6, opaque list done 7, opaque modifier
  8, translucent 9, translucent modifier 10, PVR DMA done 19,
  punchthrough done 21), with the error bank starting at bit
  0 of ISTERR (ISP out of memory, strip halt, parameter out
  of memory, OPB out of memory, TA input error, TA input
  overflow). DC-3 corrected this block's register order and
  summary bits against the official documentation; see the
  DC-3 section.
* `pvr`: the PowerVR2 (CLX2). Register file (ID, REVISION,
  SOFTRESET, STARTRENDER, PARAM_BASE, REGION_BASE, VO_BORDER_COL,
  FB_R_CTRL, FB_W_CTRL, FB_W_LINESTRIDE, FB_R_SOF1/2, FB_R_SIZE,
  FB_W_SOF1/2, FB_X_CLIP, FB_Y_CLIP, ISP_BACKGND_T/S/D,
  ISP_FEED_CFG, FPU_SHAD_SCALE, SDRAM_CFG, FPU_CULL_MODE, fog
  registers, the SPG registers, TEXT_CONTROL, VO_CONTROL,
  VO_STARTX/Y, SCALER_CTL, PAL_RAM_CTRL, FPU_PARAM_CFG,
  HALF_OFFSET, FPU_PERP_VAL, SPG_STATUS, TA_ITP_CURRENT,
  TA_OL_BASE, TA_ISP_BASE, TA_OL_LIMIT, TA_ISP_LIMIT,
  TA_GLOB_TILE_CLIP, TA_ALLOC_CTRL, TA_LIST_INIT, TA_LIST_CONT,
  TA_YUV_TEX_BASE/CTRL/CNT, TA_NEXT_OPB, TA_NEXT_OPB_INIT),
  palette RAM (4 KB, PAL_RAM_CTRL formats 1555, 565, 4444, 8888),
  the fog table (stored; see the fog note below), the TA
  parameter parser, and the tile renderer.
* SPG: the beam advances by exact fractions (pixel clock 27 MHz,
  or 13.5 MHz when FB_R_CTRL selects the divided clock, against
  the 200 MHz cycle stream; no floating point drift). Vblank in
  and out fire on the lines SPG_VBLANK_INT names, hblank fires
  per SPG_HBLANK_INT, and SPG_STATUS reports scanline, hblank
  window, vblank, and field live. Power-on defaults are the
  documented NTSC totals (858 by 263).
* TA: parameter streams arrive through the TA FIFO window at
  0x00500000 (and the YUV FIFO at 0x00600000). The parser handles
  end of list, user tile clip, and control parameters, polygon
  and modifier volume headers, sprite headers, and vertex
  parameters (type 1 packed, with and without UV16, plus
  two-volume and sprite forms), building the five display lists
  (opaque, opaque modifier, translucent, translucent modifier,
  punchthrough). Completed primitives are also written into
  VRAM as ISP parameter blocks at TA_ISP_BASE with per-tile OPB
  chain entries at TA_OL_BASE under the TA_ALLOC_CTRL budgets;
  overflows raise the documented Holly error bits. The TA YUV
  converter turns 384-byte macroblocks (BT.601) into twiddled
  RGB565 texture in VRAM and raises the YUV done event.
* Renderer (on STARTRENDER): region array walk with per-tile
  list disables, background plane first (color from
  ISP_BACKGND_S, depth from ISP_BACKGND_D), then the lists in
  hardware order (opaque, opaque modifier, punchthrough,
  translucent modifier, translucent), all eight ISP depth modes,
  FPU culling modes, perspective-correct interpolation of
  inverse depth, UV, and color, modifier volumes as a per-pixel
  counter (inside parity selects the second parameter set of
  two-volume primitives and the shading of translucent modifier
  lists), texturing in 1555, 565, 4444, 8888, YUV422, paletted 4
  and 8 bit, and VQ compressed forms, twiddled, linear, and
  stride layouts, mipmaps, point and bilinear filtering, the
  replace, modulate, decal, and shadow texture instructions,
  punchthrough alpha test against ALPHA_REF, and full src/dst
  blend factor blending for the translucent lists. Output goes
  into VRAM at FB_W_SOF1 in the FB_W_CTRL format (0555, 0565,
  0888, 8888) with the hardware Bayer 4x4 ordered dither when
  enabled, FB_X_CLIP/FB_Y_CLIP scissoring, and
  FB_W_LINESTRIDE strides. Render done raises the ISP then TSP
  Holly events. `Machine.Framebuffer` presents the read
  framebuffer at FB_R_SOF1 converted to XRGB8888 per FB_R_CTRL
  and FB_R_SIZE.

## DC-3: what is in this slice

Sound (the AICA with its own ARM7TDMI), the Maple controller
bus, G2 DMA, and the fog unit deferred from DC-2.

* Correction to DC-2: the Holly register order and the ISTNRM
  summary bits shipped in DC-2 contradicted the official
  documentation. The documented map is SB_ISTNRM at
  0x005F6900, SB_ISTEXT at +0x04, SB_ISTERR at +0x08 (masks
  IML2NRM/EXT/ERR at 0x6910/14/18, IML4 at 0x6920/24/28, IML6
  at 0x6930/34/38), and in ISTNRM bit 31 is the error summary
  and bit 30 the external summary. DC-2 had ISTERR and ISTEXT
  swapped and the summary bits exchanged; both are fixed,
  with the bank indices and the serialized layout unchanged.
  One known deviation remains: the event id for PVR DMA done
  is still the DC-2 value 19, while the official table puts
  PVR DMA end at bit 11 and channel 2 DMA end at bit 19;
  nothing raises the event yet, so the discrepancy is inert.
* `chips/arm7`: the AICA's ARM7TDMI, this module's own
  implementation (ARM and Thumb states, mode banking,
  IRQ/FIQ/undefined/SWI/abort exceptions, the GBATEK cycle
  model). Gated by the Tom Harte ARM7TDMI corpus, copied
  local-only into `testroms/` like the other cores (never
  committed): the default harness subset passes 90,000 of
  90,000 (2,000 per file across all 45 files), and the full
  corpus at `DC_TH_SUBSET=50000` passes 2,250,000 of
  2,250,000. Coprocessor instructions raise the undefined
  exception, matching the corpus states; data aborts cannot
  occur because the bus interface cannot fault. One corpus
  quirk is pinned in the Thumb unit: a POP with an empty
  register list transfers only the program counter, and the
  loaded value keeps its bit 0 visible in R15, while a
  listed POP into the program counter masks it; the
  reference states distinguish the two paths.
* `aica`: the sound block. 64 channels with the documented
  register file: start address with format select (16-bit
  PCM, 8-bit PCM, 4-bit Yamaha ADPCM with the published step
  table and per-channel predictor and step state), loop
  start/end, key on/off through the common KYONEX write,
  OCT/FNS pitch at the 44,100 Hz base, the AICA envelope
  generator (attack, decay 1, decay 2, release with the
  documented rate tables and sustain level), pitch and
  amplitude LFO, DISDL/DIPAN direct sends, ISEL/IMXL effect
  sends, Q with a one-pole lowpass filter, and the position
  and envelope monitor readback. Samples step at exactly
  512 master cycles (22.5792 MHz master, 44,100 Hz). The
  ARM7 runs at half the master clock, 11.2896 MHz, the rate
  the DC documentation gives for the sound CPU. The DSP
  effect unit executes the documented 128-step microprogram
  (COEF, MADRS, MPRO loaded through registers; TEMP, MEMS,
  MIXS, EFREG data paths with the documented multiply, add,
  shift, pack and unpack operations), gated on a hand built
  gain plus feedback delay program against hand computed
  outputs. Common registers cover MVOL, the three timers
  (sample-clocked interrupt sources), the internal register
  DMA, the RTC, the MIDI stub port, the ARM/SH-4 shared
  registers, the interrupt controller both ways (level
  presentation with end of interrupt to the ARM as FIQ; the
  SH-4 path raises the Holly external AICA bit), and the
  ARMRST control that holds and releases the ARM7.
* `maple`: the controller bus. SB_MDSTAR points at a command
  table in main RAM; SB_MDST (with SB_MDEN) runs it
  synchronously, or SB_MDTSEL defers it to vblank out. Frames
  follow the documented format (command, recipient, sender,
  word count, payload). Two devices per port: the standard
  controller (Device Info with the documented function code
  and function data, Get Condition fed by `SetButtons`:
  buttons in the documented wire bit layout, active low,
  triggers and stick axes) and a VMU-like storage device on
  the sub address (MemoryCard function, 128 KB image, 512
  byte blocks, Get Block and Write Block). Unknown commands
  answer 0xFE, known commands with an unsupported function
  answer 0xFC with the function word, bad block requests
  answer 0xFB, and an empty sub address receives the single
  word 0xFFFFFFFF. Completion raises the Holly Maple DMA
  done event (ISTNRM bit 12, verified against the published
  table).
* `g2dma`: the G2 DMA controller at 0x005F7800. The AICA
  channel copies synchronously in both directions between
  system memory and AICA space (the documented length is the
  byte count), raising ISTNRM bit 15 and the AICA-side DMA
  end interrupt. The Ext1, Ext2, and Dev channels model
  absent devices: started transfers set their busy bit and
  never complete, which is the documented behavior of a DMA
  to a device that is not there.
* Fog (closes the DC-2 deferral): all four documented TSP
  fog modes are applied in the shading stage after the
  source color clamp: table fog through the 128 entry table
  at window +0x200 with FOG_COL_RAM and the FOG_DENSITY
  mantissa and exponent format, per-vertex fog with
  FOG_COL_VERT keyed on the interpolated offset alpha (and
  the Offset bit), no fog, and Look Up Table Mode 2. The
  gate mixes a known depth against a hand filled table to
  the exact presented pixel.
* `system`: RunFrame steps the AICA in scanline chunks by
  the exact rational ratio (SH-4 cycles times 225792 over
  2000000), `AudioBuffer()` drains stereo at 44,100 Hz, and
  `SetButtons` now feeds the Maple controller on port 0.
  The whole-machine gate runs one program through all of
  it: the SH-4 copies and releases an ARM sound driver, the
  driver keys a looping PCM channel and takes timer FIQs,
  a Maple condition poll lands and vectors its handler, the
  fog scene renders, and a mid-run save restores to a byte
  identical continuation including audio.

### DC-3 simplifications and boundaries

* The DSP coefficient for the filter Q is a stated model:
  the documentation gives the Q table in dB (0.75 dB per
  step, minus 3 dB) but no coefficient formula for the
  one-pole section, so the resonant gain follows that table
  directly and Q = 4 with FLV at maximum is exactly
  transparent, the documented pass-through setting.
* Noise generation (SSCTL) is a per-channel xorshift LFSR;
  the hardware noise algorithm is not in the published
  documentation used here. The position monitor returns the
  low 16 bits of the sample position. MIDI is a stub (the
  out interrupt fires on a buffer write, input never
  arrives). The DSP external inputs EXTS are silent (no
  external source exists in this machine), and DSP TABLE
  addressing is absolute into wave RAM rather than ring
  relative. The RTC write model uses a simplified enable
  latch. The ARM/SH-4 wave RAM write-protect bit (RP) is
  stored, not enforced.
* Maple models the controller and the storage sub-device
  only; other documented devices (keyboard, mouse, gun,
  microphone) are not implemented, and their addresses
  answer as empty. All Status returns the Device Info
  payload plus the condition words, a documented layout
  choice. SB_MDAPRO is stored without checking the
  documented security code. Function codes are carried in
  the RAM representation used by the public headers
  (controller 0x01000000, storage 0x02000000); the Dev.Box
  worked example prints the controller code byte-reversed,
  which this core treats as a documentation artifact.
* G2 interrupt-triggered DMA (TSEL other than 0) is not
  modeled; the trigger mask registers sit outside the
  Holly window. The G2 read counters report start plus
  length and a zero remaining length after the synchronous
  AICA copy. SB_G2ID reads 0.
* Interrupts from the AICA to the SH-4 are level presented
  from the shared pending word; because the machine steps
  the two CPUs in chunks, an AICA source the ARM
  acknowledges inside the same chunk (its own timer FIQ)
  never becomes visible to the SH-4. The DC-3 gate
  therefore counts timer B on the SH-4 side, which the ARM
  never acknowledges. On hardware the two CPUs run
  concurrently and both would see the line.



| Range | Contents |
| :--- | :--- |
| 0x00000000 to 0x001FFFFF | BIOS window, HLE NOP sled plus the handler stub page at 0x800 (see the DC-4 section) |
| 0x00200000 to 0x002FFFFF | Flash ROM, 256 KB mirrored across the window |
| 0x00500000 to 0x005FFFFF | TA FIFO (polygon parameter stream) |
| 0x005F6900 to 0x005F693F | Holly interrupt block (real behavior) |
| 0x005F6C00 to 0x005F6CFF | Maple controller bus (real behavior) |
| 0x005F7000 to 0x005F70FF | GD-ROM registers (stub storage) |
| 0x005F7800 to 0x005F78FF | G2 DMA controller (real behavior) |
| 0x005F8000 to 0x005F9FFF | PowerVR registers, palette RAM, fog table (real behavior) |
| 0x00600000 to 0x00600FFF | YUV FIFO (macroblock stream) |
| 0x00601000 to 0x006FFFFF | Modem and expansion area (stub storage, idle) |
| 0x00700000 to 0x00707FFF | AICA registers (real behavior) |
| 0x00710000 to 0x0071000B | AICA RTC (real behavior) |
| 0x00800000 to 0x009FFFFF | AICA RAM, 2 MB |
| 0x04000000 to 0x04FFFFFF | VRAM 32-bit view, 8 MB mirrored |
| 0x05000000 to 0x05FFFFFF | VRAM 64-bit view, 8 MB mirrored, bank interleaved (below) |
| 0x0C000000 to 0x0FFFFFFF | Main RAM, 16 MB mirrored |

Register stubs are plain stored words: a read returns the last
32-bit value written to that exact aligned address (default 0),
and byte or half writes merge into the stored word.

The VRAM 64-bit window interleaves the two 4 MB VRAM banks the
way the hardware does: an 8-byte unit in the 64-bit window takes
its low word from bank 0 and its high word from bank 1 at the
same row offset (backing + 0x400000). Twiddled textures uploaded
through this window therefore land exactly where the renderer's
twiddle addressing expects them, which the test suite proves
end to end with a textured quad submitted over the bus.

Interlace presentation: when SPG_CONTROL selects interlace, the
presented frame composes both fields: even rows come from
FB_R_SOF1 and odd rows from FB_R_SOF2, each field holding half
the lines at the same stride, while the SPG field bit flips per
field. Progressive output reads FB_R_SOF1 only.

## DC-4: what is in this slice

The BIOS HLE boot, the libretro shell, the enginetest gate, and
the app wiring preparation. With this slice the core is
complete: a disc image boots end to end through our own BIOS
high-level emulation, plays through the shell, and passes the
shared engine test.

### The boot model

`Machine.BootDisc` performs the machine side of the documented
Dreamcast boot sequence:

* The disc's IP.BIN (the first 16 sectors of the data area,
  32 KB) is read through the `gd` layer and validated with the
  DC-1 parser (`gd.ParseIPBin`); an absent or malformed IP.BIN
  fails the boot with a clean error before the CPU is touched.
* The IP image is copied to its documented load address
  0x8C008000. The BIOS variables page (0x8C000000 to
  0x8C001000) is cleared, then the documented syscall vector
  table is written: sysinfo at 0x8C0000B0, ROM font at
  0x8C0000B4, flashrom at 0x8C0000B8, GD-ROM at 0x8C0000BC and
  0x8C0000C0, system boot at 0x8C0000E0, and the GD-ROM direct
  entry pointer at 0x8C0010F0. The SYSINFO id block at
  0x8C000068 stays zeroed: the real BIOS copies it from the
  flash sysinfo partition, which this core does not model.
* The CPU enters the IP at 0x8C008300 with SP 0x8C00F000 (the
  boot stack region the public boot documentation places just
  below the 0x8C00F000 vector and scratch block) and PR 0. SR
  keeps its power-on value; a real IP sets its own SR, VBR,
  and stack as its first act, and the fixture IP does exactly
  that.

No BIOS bytes are embedded or executed. The vector slots point
at handler stubs in the BIOS window: one page at physical
0x800, written by us, holding eight stubs of eight bytes each
(RTS, NOP, NOP, NOP). The machine intercepts execution when
the program counter reaches a stub, services the call in Go,
and returns through PR; the stub's own RTS is a safety net for
execution arriving by any other path.

### The syscall subset

The implemented subset is what a boot IP needs, at the
documented vectors, with the documented GD request model
(REQ_CMD returns a request id or 0 while busy, EXEC_SERVER
executes, GET_CMD_STAT reports busy, complete, or error with
the result words):

* GD-ROM (vector 0x8C0000BC and 0x8C0000C0, R6 = 0): REQ_CMD,
  GET_CMD_STAT, EXEC_SERVER, INIT_SYSTEM, GET_DRV_STAT, and
  RESET. Commands: PIOREAD and DMAREAD (FAD addressed sector
  reads through the `gd` layer; result word 0 is bytes
  transferred), GETTOC2 (the session and track table),
  INIT, GET_VERSION (this HLE's own banner, never a Sega
  string), GETSCD (a zeroed subcode block), and PLAY, PLAY2,
  PAUSE, RELEASE completing at once (no CD audio model).
* Misc (same vector, R6 = -1): INIT.
* SYSINFO (0x8C0000B0): init, and the id block read (zeroed,
  see above).
* System boot (0x8C0000E0): function 0, the exit to the BIOS
  menu. There is no menu in this HLE, so the CPU halts and
  the machine idles on its last frame.

Everything else (the font and flashrom vectors in full, the
remaining GD functions and commands, further sysinfo and
system functions) is a logged stub: it returns the
documented error shape (0xFFFFFFFF, or the GD error status)
and is recorded in `Machine.UnimplementedBIOSCalls`, with a
summary (`Machine.BIOSDiagnostics`) the shell prints through
the frontend log at unload, the PS1 core's pattern. Handlers
preserve every register except R0. The requests execute
synchronously at EXEC_SERVER, so a poll loop sees busy only
when no request was queued. One read is bounded to 8192
sectors.

Two boundaries of the boot model, stated plainly: the boot
file is served as stored, so the retail descramble step is
not implemented and unscrambled (homebrew layout) images are
the supported form; and retail discs' own IP.BIN programs are
Sega code this repository does not contain, so a retail image
boots only as far as its IP runs on this syscall subset (see
the honesty notes). No retail game has been booted on this
core yet.

### The enginetest gate

`system/dc4_test.go` builds a synthetic disc (.gdi and .iso
forms) whose IP.BIN is a hand-assembled SH-4 program (a small
two-pass assembler in the test file; every encoding is the
documented one) that does the real boot work through the BIOS
calls: GD init, GETTOC2, a PVD read, an ISO9660 root walk
that finds the boot file named in its own header, and sector
by sector PIOREAD loads of the payload to 0x8C010000. The
payload keys the DC-3 ARM7 sound driver tone, polls Maple
port 0 through a DMA table, renders the DC-2 textured quad
scene, arms the vblank interrupt, and idles on SLEEP while
its handler counts vblanks. Milestones land in order at
0x8C300000, all inside the first frame.

Gate results (2026-10-13): all five milestones observed in
frame 0, in order; framebuffer probes exact (0xF800, 0x07E0,
0x8400, 0x001F, 0xFFFF raw, and the presented red texel
0xFFFF0000 and bilinear midpoint 0xFF848200); the recorded
Maple condition words match the host pad state exactly
(0x07002003, 0x01000000, 0xFFF300C8, 0x8080C81E for A and
Start pressed, trigger 200, stick (30, 200)); the tone's
period is found verbatim in the drained audio and measures
exactly 64.00 samples (689 Hz at 44100 Hz) over 46 rising
edges; the boot used zero unimplemented BIOS calls; a
mid-run save restores byte-identical continuation (state,
framebuffer, and audio). The same disc through the built
desktop core (`builds/libgo_dc_desktop.so`) in the shared
harness (`go_backend/cmd/enginetest`): ALL TESTS PASSED
(640x480 non-blank video, non-silent audio, save state
28,162,901 bytes with the scene loaded, restore frame hash
equal). Debugging the gate caught three real fixture bugs
worth naming: an LDS encoding mixup (PR vs MACH), and the
two SH-4 delay slot traps (a conditional branch's delay slot
runs only when taken; a call's delay slot reads pre-call
registers).

### The shell

`libretro` follows the family pattern: core name
"iTaK GoDC", extensions `gdi|iso|bin` (the `gd` layer has no
.cue parser, so cue is not advertised), `need_fullpath` set
(a .gdi resolves its track files relative to its own
directory), geometry fixed at the PVR Present output
640x480, XRGB8888. The declared fps is the quotient of the
machine's own documented constants, 200,000,000 Hz over the
3,333,333 cycle frame budget = 60.000006, not the 59.94
NTSC figure: the core's flat model runs at 60, and the shell
says so. Audio is the AICA's native 44,100 Hz stereo. The
pad maps the libretro standard layout to the DC pad (A, B,
X, Y, Start, dpad), the analog triggers from the libretro
analog button axes (L2 and R2) with a digital full-press
fallback from L and R, and the main stick from the left
analog axes scaled to 0..255 with 128 centered; through the
iTaK Go bridge (digital joypad only) the stick reads
centered and the triggers read through L and R.
RETRO_MEMORY_SYSTEM_RAM is the 16 MB main RAM;
RETRO_MEMORY_SAVE_RAM is port 0's live 128 KB VMU image.
Serialize goes through the system save states; reset
reboots the loaded disc.

### Fixes and wiring state

* The Holly PVR DMA done event constant is corrected to the
  documented table value 11 (DC-2 and DC-3 carried 19, the
  channel-2 DMA end value). A module-wide grep before the
  fix found the declaration as the constant's only use;
  nothing raised or tested it, so the fix is free. There is
  still no PVR DMA to raise it.
* App wiring preparation is done locally and NOT pushed:
  `go_backend/internal/core/types.go` (the Cores64BitOnly
  Dreamcast entry is now "iTaK GoDC" / libgo_dc.so with
  extensions gdi, iso, bin) and `flutter_ui/lib/main.dart`
  (the 'dc' entry uses libgo_dc.so with the same extensions;
  `requires64: true` unchanged). `tools/autobuild-server.sh`
  is untouched: it has no 64-bit branch, which is the
  parent's pipeline task.

## Save states

`Machine.Serialize` writes, in order:

1. One version byte, currently 0x04.
2. The CPU state (`sh4.SerializeSize` bytes, which now includes
   the latched pending interrupt).
3. Main RAM, then VRAM, then flash, then AICA RAM, each at its
   live length.
4. The Holly block (48 bytes: three status words, nine mask
   words).
5. The PVR state: registers, palette RAM, fog table, the SPG
   beam position (exact fractional accumulator included), and
   the TA scene: parser state, YUV converter progress, and the
   display lists not held in VRAM. The section size varies with
   the scene, and `StateSize` reports the current exact total.
6. The AICA state: the raw register file, the DSP memories,
   every channel's runtime state, the interrupt controller,
   the output ring, and the ARM7 CPU state.
7. The Maple state: registers, the four pad states, and the
   four 128 KB VMU images.
8. The G2 DMA registers and channel state, then a 16 byte
   machine tail: the AICA clock accumulator remainder and
